sections.heading: The AI-factory landlord model
bullets: The landlord builds and owns the building, power connection, and cooling plant; the tenant brings the GPUs. Rent is a 15-year take-or-pay lease — paid whether or not the tenant uses the capacity

Lease economics benchmark: roughly $1.6-1.8M of rent per critical-IT megawatt per year, against ~$10M+ per MW to build — a ~6-7 year payback before financing costs, with decades of contract left after
The 'franchise model' idea: standardize the design, the supplier contracts, and the construction playbook so each new campus is a copy, not a project — speed and cost-certainty become the product
Why tenants accept 15-year lock-ins: power and permitted land are the scarce inputs; a signed lease on an already-connected site beats years in an interconnection queue

sections.heading: Why cold, windy nowhere wins: siting economics
bullets: PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) is total facility power ÷ IT power; every 0.1 of PUE on 100 MW is ~10 MW of pure overhead. A 1.18 design vs the ~1.5 global average is tens of millions of dollars a year
Free cooling: in a cold climate the outside air (or a dry cooler loop) removes heat 200+ days per year with no chillers running — the single biggest PUE lever

Waterless direct-to-chip cooling: a closed liquid loop touches cold plates on the chips, rejected to dry coolers — near-zero water use (WUE ~0) removes the community objection that kills permits elsewhere
Cheap rural power grids (like the northern plains) offer both low prices and available interconnection capacity — the two things AI campuses queue years for in Virginia or Texas

sections.heading: Reading revenue quality: rent vs fit-out
bullets: AI landlord revenue has two very different lines: base rent (recurring, high-margin, contract-backed — the valuable kind) and tenant fit-out (one-time construction/services revenue recognized while customizing space — lumpy and pass-through-like)
Fit-out can dwarf rent during buildout quarters: a single quarter can recognize $150M+ of fit-out against $45M of base rent — making 'revenue' triple without the recurring business tripling
This is why consensus beats can be meaningless here: analysts can't time fit-out recognition, so 50-150% 'beats' say more about accounting timing than about performance
The metric that cuts through: NOI (net operating income) — rent minus property operating costs — and its margin (~90% for a well-run AI campus). Track NOI run-rate, not revenue

sections.heading: The capital stack of a building spree
bullets: Project-level notes: bonds issued by a subsidiary that owns one campus, secured by that campus's lease — the debt is quarantined, and each new lease can be financed separately (coupons compress as the developer proves delivery: 9.25% → 6.75% in months)

Perpetual preferred equity: mezzanine capital with no maturity — pays a high dividend (12-13%, often PIK: paid in more preferred instead of cash), and can carry a minimum-return multiple (e.g., 1.80x MOIC) plus a slice of the business's common equity
PIK (payment-in-kind) means the obligation compounds instead of consuming cash today — friendly to construction cash flow, expensive to eventual equity value

The sequencing logic: expensive, flexible capital (preferred, bridges) starts construction; cheap, rigid capital (project notes at tighter coupons) takes it out once leases are signed and buildings deliver

sections.heading: Concentration and the unnamed tenant problem
bullets: Two counterparties can be 100% of a landlord's revenue — then credit analysis of the tenants matters more than analysis of the landlord
Hyperscalers often demand anonymity in leases ('a US-based investment-grade hyperscaler') — the market must underwrite billions of backlog against a counterparty it cannot name or verify
A neocloud anchor tenant (itself leveraged, itself dependent on its own customers) is a weaker credit than a hyperscaler — landlords manage this with restructured guarantees and letters of credit
ROFR (right of first refusal) clauses matter: a tenant holding ROFR on a campus's remaining capacity effectively controls its growth path without paying for it yet

sections.heading: Separating businesses to clarify value
bullets: A GPU cloud (short contracts, fast depreciation, tech risk) and a lease landlord (15-year contracts, real-estate risk) deserve different valuation multiples — housing both in one ticker muddies each
Spinning the cloud into its own listed company (while retaining most of the equity) gives the market a clean landlord to price and a separate mark for the cloud stake
Watch what stays behind: legacy bitcoin hosting can be kept purely as a cash yield on depreciated assets — not strategy, just funding
Adjacency investments (a stake in a gas-generation developer, a cooling-technology startup) are options on the landlord's own future constraints: power timing and rack density

flashcards.q: In the AI-factory landlord model, who owns what?
flashcards.a: The landlord owns the building, grid connection, and cooling plant; the tenant installs and owns the GPUs. Rent is a multi-year take-or-pay lease on the critical-IT megawatts.

flashcards.q: Rough landlord math: what does a megawatt earn vs cost?
flashcards.a: About $1.6-1.8M of lease revenue per critical-IT MW per year against ~$10M+ per MW to build — a 6-7 year pre-financing payback with a 15-year contract behind it.

flashcards.q: Why does a 1.18 PUE beat a 1.5 PUE by tens of millions a year?
flashcards.a: PUE is facility power ÷ IT power. On a 100 MW IT load, 1.5 means 50 MW of overhead vs 18 MW at 1.18 — 32 MW of round-the-clock electricity saved, plus the capex for that equipment.

flashcards.q: What is free cooling and where do you get it?
flashcards.a: Rejecting heat to cold outside air without running chillers. Cold-climate sites get 200+ free-cooling days a year — the biggest single lever on PUE.

flashcards.q: What makes 'waterless' cooling a permitting weapon?
flashcards.a: Closed-loop direct-to-chip cooling rejected through dry coolers uses near-zero water (WUE ~0). Water draw is a top community objection to data centers — removing it removes a veto point.

flashcards.q: Base rent vs tenant fit-out revenue — which matters?
flashcards.a: Base rent is recurring, ~90%-margin, contract-backed. Fit-out is one-time construction revenue recognized during customization — lumpy and low-quality. Value the rent; treat fit-out as noise.

flashcards.q: Why are consensus beats a weak signal for AI landlords in buildout?
flashcards.a: Analysts can't time fit-out revenue recognition, so quarters 'beat' by 50-150% on accounting timing. NOI run-rate and MW energized on schedule are the real scorecard.

flashcards.q: What is a project-level note and why quarantine debt per campus?
flashcards.a: A bond issued by the subsidiary owning one campus, secured by its lease. Each campus finances itself, default risk doesn't cross-contaminate, and coupons compress as the developer proves delivery.

flashcards.q: Decode: perpetual preferred at 12.75% PIK with a 1.80x MOIC floor plus 15% of the equity.
flashcards.a: No-maturity mezzanine capital whose dividend compounds in kind (no cash out now), guarantees the investor at least 1.8x their money on exit, and takes 15% ownership on top — flexible construction capital at a very steep all-in price.

flashcards.q: Why do expensive preferreds and bridges come first, cheap notes later?
flashcards.a: Before leases are signed, only flexible high-cost capital will fund construction. Once take-or-pay leases exist and buildings deliver, project notes at far tighter coupons refinance the expensive layer.

flashcards.q: What does a tenant's ROFR on the rest of a campus do?
flashcards.a: A right of first refusal lets the anchor tenant match any future offer on the remaining capacity — it controls the campus's growth path without having leased or paid for it yet.

flashcards.q: Why might a landlord demand a letter of credit from its own anchor tenant?
flashcards.a: When the tenant is a leveraged neocloud rather than an investment-grade hyperscaler, the landlord carries real counterparty risk. Restructured guarantees and an LC convert some of that promise into posted collateral.
